Lystra
LIS-truh
proper noun (place)
Greek Lystra; a city in the region of Lycaonia in Asia Minor (modern Turkey), visited by Paul on his first missionary journey. The hometown of Timothy.

See also: Lystra

Biblical Definition

Lystra was a city in Lycaonia in Asia Minor where the Apostle Paul, on his first missionary journey, healed a man crippled from birth, was hailed as a god by the pagan crowd, and then, when the crowd turned, was stoned and left for dead — and which was the hometown of his beloved disciple Timothy. When Paul preached at Lystra, he saw a man who had never walked and, perceiving his faith, commanded him to stand; the man leaped and walked (Acts 14:8-10). The pagan people of Lystra, astonished, cried out in their own language that "the gods are come down to us in the likeness of men," and called Barnabas Jupiter (Zeus) and Paul Mercurius (Hermes), and the priest of Jupiter prepared to offer sacrifice to them (Acts 14:11-13). Paul and Barnabas, horrified, rent their clothes and ran among the people, crying, "Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God" (Acts 14:15) — a model of how God's servants refuse worship and turn all glory to God. But the fickle crowd was soon turned by hostile Jews from Antioch and Iconium; they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing him dead. As the disciples stood round him, he rose up and went back into the city (Acts 14:19-20) — a striking testimony to God's preserving power and Paul's undaunted courage. Lystra teaches several lessons: the danger of misdirected worship (the crowd ready to worship men), the duty of God's servants to refuse all glory and point men to the living God, the fickleness of crowd-approval (worshipping one day, stoning the next), and the perseverance of the gospel through suffering. And Lystra gave the church Timothy, "well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium" (Acts 16:1-2), Paul's son in the faith and fellow-laborer.

Webster 1828 Definition

A city in Lycaonia where Paul healed a man crippled from birth, was hailed as the god Mercurius (with Barnabas as Jupiter) and refused the worship, then was stoned and left for dead but rose and returned (Acts 14); the hometown of Timothy (Acts 16:1-2).

LYSTRA, proper noun. Greek Lystra; a city in Lycaonia, Asia Minor; the hometown of Timothy.

Where Paul healed a man crippled from birth, perceiving his faith (Acts 14:8-10).

The pagan crowd called Barnabas Jupiter (Zeus) and Paul Mercurius (Hermes) and prepared to sacrifice to them (Acts 14:11-13).

Paul and Barnabas refused the worship, turning the people to the living God (Acts 14:15).

The fickle crowd, stirred by hostile Jews, stoned Paul and left him for dead; he rose and returned to the city (Acts 14:19-20).

Key Scripture

Acts 14:11 — "And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men."

Acts 14:15 — "And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God."

Acts 14:19-20 — "And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead. Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city."

Acts 16:1-2 — "Then came he to Derbe and Lystra: and, behold, a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus... Which was well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium."

Modern Corruption

Lystra is corrupted when the lesson of refused worship is overlooked, when the fickleness of crowd-approval is missed, or when the stoning of Paul is read apart from the perseverance of the gospel through suffering.

expand to see more

Refused-worship lesson missed. When the crowd at Lystra prepared to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods, the apostles' response is a model for every servant of God who is tempted to receive glory: they rent their clothes in horror, ran among the people, and cried, "We also are men of like passions with you" (Acts 14:15), turning all worship to the living God. In an age that builds platforms and cults of personality even within the church, the apostles' refusal of worship is a sharp rebuke. The true servant of God deflects all glory to God and refuses to let men make idols of him; he insists, "We are men like you" and points beyond himself to Christ.

Lystra has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the fickleness of crowd-approval and the perseverance of the gospel through suffering. The same crowd that one moment hailed Paul as a god, the next moment stoned him and left him for dead — a sober warning against trusting the praise of crowds, which turns as quickly to violence (as Jerusalem's "Hosanna" turned to "Crucify"). And Paul's rising from the stoning to walk back into the very city that had stoned him testifies to God's preserving power and the undaunted courage of the gospel, which presses on through suffering to plant the church — the church that would give the world Timothy.
